newsitem.title: INDIA: Kashmir hostage relatives appeal for information.
newsitem.headline: Kashmir hostage relatives appeal for information.

text.p: Two years after a shadowy guerrilla group kidnapped four Westerners in Kashmir, their relatives appealed to India, Pakistan and the people of Kashmir for clues on the captives' fate.

"I appeal to all citizens of Kashmir, to the government of Jammu and Kashmir, to the government of India and to the government of Pakistan: Please help to clarify the fate of my brother and other hostages," Birgit Hasert sister of German hostage Dirk Hasert, told a news conference on Saturday.
On July 4, 1995, Americans Donald Hutchings and John Childs and Britons Paul Wells and Keith Mangan were kidnapped by Al-Faran militants while trekking in the Himalayan state of Jammu and Kashmir.
Four days later, Childs escaped. On the same day, the captors abducted German Dirk Hasert and Norwegian Hans Christian Ostroe. Ostroe was later found beheaded.
On Friday, Hasert's sister, accompanied by Jane Schelly, wife of Donald Hutchings and Julie Mangan, wife of Briton Keith Mangan attended prayers and tied ribbons in a church and a Moslem shrine.
They jointly addressed the news conference on Saturday.
"Two years have passed and still we seek to know the truth regarding the fate of our loved ones. I believe there is someone who knows the answer on what has happened to them," Schelly said.
More than 20,000 people have been killed in a seven-year-old rebellion in Jammu and Kashmir, mainly Hindu India's only Moslem majority state.
Dozens of groups are fighting New Delhi's rule in the disputed region over which India and Pakistan have fought two wars. Pakistan denies Indian charges that it arms Kashmiri separatists.
Julie Mangan and Birgit Hasert arrived in Srinagar, Jammu and Kashmir's summer capital, earlier this week and travelled to Magam village, 85 km (53 miles) south.

Several captured guerrillas have told Indian authorities that the four hostages were executed in December 1995, one month after negotiations for their release broke down, and that they were buried in a cave in a forest near Magam.
Jane Schelly, arrived on Friday and accompanied the two other women to the city's main mosque to attend weekly prayers.
The relatives have made a number of visits over the past two years to India, Pakistan and other Western countries to press for news of the tourists.
"Whether you return to me or not, whether I find you or not, I have seen the whole world in my search for you," Schelly said, recalling her husband.
"Indeed this search has taken me so far to the mountains of Kashmir to the plains of India, to Pakistan, Norway, Washington.... but still no answers and no end." she said.
